idea: tiny CLI that prints the current moon phase, with a fun ascii moon
spec_digest: improvement run on shipped v0.1.0 moon CLI: harden tests, close known-issues, polish docs for truth - NO new features, no new runtime deps, core astronomy not rewritten
must: KI-1 closed with evidence, KI-6 fixed (consistent throw), KI-7 bounded by a declared+SAMPLED supported domain, KI-5 pinned by a measuring test
every added test closes a NAMED untested surface; test count is not an outcome
non-goals: no new flags/features, no npm publish, no dependencies, no emoji/color
taste: the risk is CHURN - one test pinning a real defect beats ten restating a pass

decisions.what: port a documented Meeus/Duffett-Smith algorithm into zero-dep Node rather than fork prior art
decisions.why: prior-art scout returned stance `extend` — the phoon lineage (Poskanzer -> moontool -> wwn-phoon-rs) is grep-verified to do real phase math offline, so re-deriving the core would be wasted work. But the cleanest candidate is Rust, which conflicts with the user's explicit node/npx/zero-install choice — and npx distribution is itself one of the three things NO prior art does. Resolution: honor `extend` in substance by porting a published algorithm and using tidecal (MIT, Meeus ch.47 in JS) as reference and wwn-phoon-rs as a cross-check oracle, while keeping the Node surface.

decisions.what: hemisphere inferred from system IANA timezone via a static table, with --south/--north override
decisions.why: hemisphere-correct art is the single differentiator verified absent in ALL prior art (moontool mirrors only its emoji; wwn-phoon-rs has zero hemisphere code). Intl exposes the TZ name offline, satisfying the no-network non-goal. Equator-straddling zones will be wrong, which is exactly what the explicit override exists for.

decisions.what: all three nice-to-haves (next-phase countdown, --date, moon age) CUT at lock
decisions.why: taste judge scored scope-fits-night 6 against the 90-minute clock and warned the accuracy claim is the thing most likely to silently slip to 'mean formula plus a few terms'. Since the entire pitch is that a wrong answer is worse than no answer, the periodic corrections must not compete for clock with optional features.

decisions.what: test_cmd set to `node --test test/*.test.js`, not `node --test test/`
decisions.why: prior run (aphorism-cli, same host, Node 24) recorded that the directory form fails with MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Adopting the known-good form at kickoff instead of rediscovering it mid-run.

decisions.what: improvement run scoped to known-issue closure + named-surface test hardening + doc truth; the original build spec is preserved (tag v0.1.0) and remains binding, this SPEC only scopes what may change
decisions.why: allocator auto-kickoff under TRICKLE posture (allow_premium_pct 0, opus_used_pct 95) with brief 'harden tests, fix playbook items, polish docs - no new features'. The stress-test's landing attack was that housekeeping's toy version is CHURN - reworded prose plus duplicate tests. The named-surface rule is the structural answer: a test that cannot name the surface it closes does not get written.

decisions.what: KI-5 (glyph East Asian Width) stays DEFERRED as a fix, but gets pinned by a measuring test this run
decisions.why: the honest fix is a glyph-set redesign (L-effort, rewrites the product's visual core). Dispatching that under gear-1 crawl with premium at 95 pct consumed is the wrong spend. Pinning the measured widths in a test converts a prose-only caveat into a machine-checked one at S-effort - the defect can no longer drift silently.

decisions.what: astronomia v4.2.0 (MIT, a genuine Meeus port in JS) found by the scout and deliberately NOT adopted as a cross-check oracle
decisions.why: zero runtime dependencies is a must-have of the original spec. Even as a devDependency it would weaken the zero-dep story for a convenience the existing hand-computed Meeus 49.a/49.b fixtures already provide.

decisions.what: T-102 and T-103 routed to sonnet, NOT flagged route_class:'core' despite playbook L-026 (route the correctness core to fable)
decisions.why: both touch src/astro.js, but neither changes the Meeus math: T-102 adds a guard clause on a return value and T-103 adds a declared constant plus a sampled test whose domain the conductor already measured. L-026 earned its keep on items requiring astronomy judgement; spending fable here under trickle posture (allow_premium_pct=0, opus_used_pct=95) would buy nothing. Recorded so the retro can check whether this call held.

decisions.what: a ladder escalation earned by a FAILED gate outranks the gear-1 demotion rule; T-101 retries at sonnet and must not be demoted back to haiku
decisions.why: the two rules collide on docs items: the routing ladder escalates haiku->sonnet after a failed attempt, while gear-1 demotion pushes docs items sonnet->haiku. Applying them in sequence returns the item to the exact tier that just produced a fabricated number, which would reproduce the defect and burn a second cycle for nothing. Escalation is a response to observed evidence about THIS item; demotion is a budget posture. Evidence wins. Recorded for the retro as a candidate playbook lesson.

decisions.what: docs items on this run get a no-unsourced-numbers gate check as a standing rule, not just for T-101
decisions.why: the improvement run's whole premise is doc truth, and the cycle-2 failure was a plausible-sounding quantity invented to make a sentence read better. A qualitative structural claim ('zero periodic corrections vs a full Meeus series') is verifiable from the repo; a magnitude is not unless it is computed in-repo and shown. Every remaining docs item (T-101 retry, T-108) is gated on this.

decisions.what: T-102 (KI-6 fix) built this cycle instead of the priority-1 T-101 docs retry
decisions.why: both are H-value S-effort must-haves, so backlog priority does not settle it and cycle.md step 4 makes value scoring the authority. The tiebreak was gate objectivity after a no-value cycle: T-102's acceptance is checkable by running the module (it throws or it does not), whereas T-101's is source-tracing prose - the same class of check that just failed. At k=1 under gear-1 crawl a cycle buys exactly one item, so it should buy the one most likely to convert to verified value. T-101 stays priority 1 and is next; its attempts counter is untouched by this deferral.

decisions.what: the cycle-2 gate's STATED reason for failing T-101 is corrected in the record: the ~4-hour figure DOES exist in-repo (README.md:156-157, REPORT.md:34, test/astro.test.js:96). The gate DECISION is upheld unchanged.
decisions.why: cycle 2 recorded 'the string 4-hour appears NOWHERE in the repo', which was a grep for the hyphenated literal only; the repo carries it in words. Leaving that in the record would have been a false premise sitting in the retro and in the item notes, and worse, a builder retrying the item would grep, find the number, and reasonably conclude the prohibition was mistaken. The real defect is narrower and survives the correction: the figure is one hand-computed datapoint for the 2000-01-06 lunation, shown with its work in README's Accuracy section, and attempt 1 lifted it into a general per-package error claim about lunarphase-js - a package nobody ran. Unsupported generalization, understating besides (largest single ch.49 periodic term ~0.40720 d ~= 9.8 h, and the terms sum). The retry brief was written WITH the correction in it, which is why attempt 2 introduced no magnitude at all instead of arguing with a premise it could disprove.

decisions.what: the no-unsourced-numbers docs gate is restated as a frame rule, not an existence rule: a quantity may appear only in the frame in which the repo already computes it
decisions.why: the cycle-2 wording ('do not quantify unless the number is computed in-repo and shown') passes attempt 1's fabrication only because that exact string was absent. It would NOT have caught the same defect written as 'nearly four hours off' - a phrasing the repo does contain, in a different frame. The frame rule catches both: a single-lunation comparison may not be re-used as a general per-package bound. Applied to T-108, which inherits the last docs work of the run.

decisions.what: T-104 (priority 4) built ahead of T-103 (priority 3, H-value) because gear 1 makes T-103 INELIGIBLE, not merely lower-value
decisions.why: Gear 1's work-choice rule allows haiku-priced work plus S-effort sonnet builds only, and T-103 is M-effort. This is a different reason from cycle 3's T-102-over-T-101 call, which was a value tiebreak between two eligible items - recording the distinction so the retro does not read a posture constraint as a judgement about T-103's worth. T-103 remains the top must-have and should be the first pick in any cycle that clears gear 1; its attempts counter is untouched. The rule also had a real cost worth naming: KI-7, a named must-have, is now waiting on a budget posture rather than on anything about the work.

decisions.what: T-104 stayed at sonnet under a gear that demotes; a test-authoring item is build-class, not docs/polish
decisions.why: Gear 1 sets demote=true, which drops non-judgment items one rung - but its sonnet->haiku step is explicitly scoped to docs/polish items, and build/fix never drops below sonnet. An item whose output is executable test code is build-class work: the cycle-2 failure showed what happens when a tier that cannot check itself is handed work whose defects are invisible to a reader. Consistent with gear 1's own 'S-effort sonnet builds only' allowance, which would be incoherent if the demotion rule then pushed those same builds to haiku.

decisions.what: T-103 (M-effort, the run's last open must-have) SPLIT into T-103a (module constant + sampled test, S) and T-103b (README sentence, S, deps on T-103a). T-103a built and verified this cycle.
decisions.why: Gear 1 allows S-effort sonnet builds only, so T-103 had been ineligible for two consecutive cycles (recorded at cycle 5) while being the only remaining must-have. Rather than let a named must-have wait on a budget posture I do not control, I decomposed it at the file boundary. The split is not a workaround dressed up as a plan: it is the better decomposition. The original ordering would have put a domain figure into README in the same item that established it, and the standing docs frame rule (cycles 2 and 4) says a quantity may appear only in the frame the repo already computes it in. Splitting with the TEST first means the README sentence in T-103b is sourced to a shipping assertion by construction rather than by a reviewer remembering to check. The split also costs nothing if the posture lifts: at gear 2+ the two slices simply run as one k=2 wave.

decisions.what: CORRECTION to the record: runfile budget.weekly.ceiling has been carrying 1 since cycle 0, which is not a value bin/swarm-budget.sh can emit. Gear 1 rests on the ALLOCATOR posture, not on the weekly governor. Gear is unchanged at 1; only the stated reason is corrected.
decisions.why: Read the script directly this cycle (reading is permitted; hard rule 5 fences writes, not reads). Its ceiling ladder is WCEIL in {5,3,2}: weekly_heat above 1.3 gives ceiling 2 plus a promote block; above 1.1 gives ceiling 3; otherwise 5. opus_heat above 1.2 sets promote_blocked ONLY, never a ceiling. Current weekly_heat = 67.0/64.38 = 1.04, below 1.1, so the script would emit ceiling 5 with promote_blocked true from opus_heat 1.49. Prior cycles conflated the allocator posture with the weekly governor and wrote a ceiling the tool has no way to produce. The gear itself is still correct at 1 (allocator posture trickle, allow_overall_pct 0, allow_premium_pct 0, dial 0.30, unchanged for six cycles), but the STATED reason was wrong, and a wrong reason in the record is what makes a later cycle reason wrongly. It matters materially: a governor ceiling would be fixed for the run, whereas an allocator posture is refreshed by the pacer and can lift. That is the difference between the claim that T-103 is permanently ineligible and the claim that it is ineligible until the posture changes. Only the second is true, and I had drafted the first before checking.

decisions.what: T-103b FAILED the gate on one clause ('confirmed by test/astro.test.js') and was reverted rather than conductor-patched, even though the repair is a single word and this is the run's last open must-have
decisions.why: Three rules pointed the same way and the cheap path violated all three. cycle.md step 6.4 is unconditional - fail means todo + attempts+1, and it does not carve out small fixes. Step 6.5 forbids opening a gate by weakening it; a conductor editing the artifact so its own gate passes is that failure mode even when the edit is honest, because nothing independent then checks the conductor's wording. And cycle 2 established on this very run that escalation is the response to observed evidence about an item - a rule that only binds when it is inexpensive is not a rule. The cost is real and named: one more k=1 cycle spent on a one-clause repair, with the run's last must-have still open. It is affordable - 22.0 h remain to stop_at - and the alternative buys a closed must-have at the price of the only mechanism keeping doc claims honest.

decisions.what: the gate's decisive check was a HEDGE-PARITY comparison against the module and test, not a reading of the prose
decisions.why: 'Confirmed' vs 'sampled' is exactly the kind of judgement that dissolves into taste if argued as wording, and I would have been arguing it against an agent self-report that explicitly claimed 'frame rule respected'. Mechanising it settled it: extract the hedge vocabulary actually present in src/astro.js's doc comment ('sampl', 'not proven', 'no contradiction', 'stride') and in test/astro.test.js (comment line 386 'This SAMPLES -- never exhaustively sweeps --', test name ending '(sampled)'), then check whether ANY of it survived into the added README text. None did, and 'confirmed' appeared instead. That makes the finding reproducible by anyone, and it produced the falsifiability discriminator that justifies the fail: if the implementation were wrong at an unsampled instant inside the domain, the module comment stays true and the README sentence becomes false. Generalisable beyond this item - a docs claim may be checked against the hedge vocabulary of the code it documents.

decisions.what: wave autotune read this as the REVERTED branch, not as 'any other outcome': k_current 4 -> 3, wave_streak 0
decisions.why: At k=1 the run dispatches into the working tree rather than a branch (recorded cycle 6), so a failed gate reverts with `git checkout` - cycle 6 recorded that this gives the same guarantee as dropping a branch, and the equivalence has to hold in both directions or it is just a convenience. One failed verify out of one item dispatched is a 100% failure rate for the wave. Also corrects an overhang cycle 6 flagged against itself: k_current had climbed to 4 on two clean k=1 waves, ahead of anything this run has actually exercised, while the gear cap of 1 is what binds. No practical effect this cycle - min(3, gear cap 1) is still 1.

decisions.what: T-103b PASSED on attempt 2; the two gate flags that fired were both defects in my own gate script and were fixed in the instrument, never by relaxing the standard
decisions.why: C1 (scope) fired because .trim() strips git porcelain's leading status-column space so my anchored regex missed, and then fired a second time because my OWN evidence file (.swarm/runs/cycle-008-verify-T-103b.txt) showed up as untracked inside the fence I was measuring. C4b fired on the word 'guarantees' in 'nothing guarantees they stay in step' - a NEGATED guarantee, which is the hedge itself and is lifted near-verbatim from src/astro.js. A blunt regex with no polarity handling would have failed the run's last must-have for using the module's own words. The distinction that matters: cycle.md step 6.5 forbids opening a gate by WEAKENING it, and none of these edits weaken anything - C4b got STRICTER (clause-split with negation handling), and I added C4c, which cross-checks that the negated-guarantee construction actually exists in the module, so my allowance cannot be something I invented to let the item through. An instrument that cannot tell a claim from its negation is not measuring the standard; repairing it is not lowering the bar.

decisions.what: the British 'behaviour' in the landed paragraph was filed as T-111, not patched by the conductor and not used to fail the item
decisions.why: Measured first rather than argued: across HEAD's README.md + src/astro.js + test/astro.test.js, 'behavior' appears 1x and 'behaviour' 0x, so this genuinely is the repo's first British spelling - a real inconsistency, not a preference. But T-103b's acceptance is domain figures + consequence + sampled-test attribution, and all three passed; failing the run's last open must-have over one letter is gate inflation, and cycle 7 already recorded that wording arguments dissolve into taste unless mechanised. Nor did I fix it myself: cycle 7 established that a conductor editing the artifact leaves nothing independent checking the conductor's wording, and a rule that only binds when the repair is expensive is not a rule. Same disposition as T-110, found at the cycle-7 gate under identical circumstances.

decisions.what: KI-7 stays in known_issues at severity low with documented_cycle 8; it was NOT moved to resolved_issues even though its must-have is now satisfied
decisions.why: The SPEC must-have reads 'KI-7 bounded by a declared+SAMPLED supported domain', and that is now true in both halves - module constant plus sampled test at cycle 6, README statement at cycle 8. But the underlying defect is untouched: the ch.49 and ch.48 series still diverge at absurd epochs, nothing enforces the domain at runtime (deliberately - a runtime guard is a behavior change the non-goals forbid), and the bound is sampled-clean rather than proven. Moving it to resolved_issues would let the morning report read as though a bug had been fixed when what actually happened is that an unbounded unknown became a bounded, documented, machine-checked one. Those are different things and the record should not blur them.

decisions.what: T-109 stays at sonnet on attempt 2 rather than escalating to opus, because the ladder escalation and the gear-1 demotion exactly cancel here
decisions.why: the ladder sends a failed sonnet item to opus; gear-1 crawl demotes opus back to sonnet. Unlike the cycle-2 collision, cancelling here does NOT return the item to the tier that just failed - sonnet is already one rung above T-109's haiku table row (docs/S), and the item has never been attempted at haiku. The substance also points the same way: attempt 1 did not fail on capability. It produced a careful, well-argued edit and failed because it rewrote a scope clause it was never asked to touch, creating a contradiction with its own new paragraph. A bigger model does not prevent an unnecessary rewrite; a brief that says 'do not widen the opening scope noun, and here is exactly how attempt 1 broke' does. Attempt 2 got that brief and passed 12/12. Recorded so the retro can check whether cheap-retry-with-a-sharper-brief is a real pattern or a lucky call.

decisions.what: the run's ONE review-fix pass is deferred again under gear-1 trickle; a single verified backlog item was bought instead
decisions.why: phase is REVIEW and the review-fix pass is the one step-4 gate this improvement run has not run. It is also the most premium-heavy work type in the pipeline - opus reviewers plus fable adversarial verifiers, three stages - dispatched as direct Agent calls because Workflow is review-gated headless. The allocator has held allow_premium_pct at 0 with opus_used_pct at 96 for nine consecutive cycles. Deferring is defensible on more than cost: every remaining backlog item (T-105, T-108, T-110, T-111, T-112, T-113) was FOUND BY A CONDUCTOR GATE, which is review-fix's own output shape, so the marginal finding rate of a formal pass is lower here than the gates are already delivering for free. This is a deferral with a reason, not an omission - the morning report must say the review-fix pass was NOT RUN.

decisions.what: the C5b gate flag was traced to my own instrument and the instrument was repaired, not the standard lowered
decisions.why: C5b required the section to state that the round limbs' EAW class is unestablished. It scoped that search to sentences literally re-naming the round limbs, so it was blind to the anaphoric chain that actually carries the hedge ('These are...', 'their East Asian Width class'). Paragraph scope is simply the correct scope for an anaphoric claim; sentence scope was wrong. Guarding against self-serving repair the way cycle 8 did: the same widening made the no-EAW-assertion check STRICTER (it now reads sentences run 1 never saw), and I added a binding test - the hedge must carry a back-reference, follow the introducing mention, have no competing subject between, and be about the EAW class specifically - so the allowance for anaphora is itself checked rather than asserted.

decisions.what: wave autotune counts cycle 9 as a REVERTED wave: k_current 3 -> 2, wave_streak 1 -> 0
decisions.why: one cycle is one autotune event, and cycle 9 as a whole contained a discarded builder diff (attempt 1, reverted with git checkout after the gate reproduced its contradiction). The rule keys on a reverted merge, and a direct-Agent tree edit thrown away is the same event as a reverted branch merge - the no-worktree headless dispatch changes the mechanism, not the outcome. Counting only the successful second dispatch would launder a two-attempt cycle into a clean one. No practical effect either way: min(k_current, gear cap 1) = 1.

decisions.what: T-112 filed at priority 4 - ahead of every remaining test item - because this cycle created it
decisions.why: landing T-109 falsified test/render.test.js:586-588, which asserts in prose that the README 'never mentions' the round limbs. The test's assertion still passes, so nothing is red and nothing would ever surface it; that is exactly why it needs to outrank work that has merely been missing since v0.1.0. A falsehood a run introduces is worse than a gap a run inherits, because the run is the reason a reader would trust it.

decisions.what: T-108 dispatched at haiku (the routing table's route for docs/S) rather than overridden upward, after the conductor pre-decided both judgment calls the item carried
decisions.why: The item's notes handed it two open questions - which resolved-status convention to adopt, and how to dispose of README's unsourced 'hours to days' magnitude - and the routing rules say a judgment call about correctness or honesty should not be cheap-tiered. Rather than spend a premium tier under trickle posture (allow_premium_pct 0, opus_used_pct 96), the conductor DECIDED both in the brief (status column with three permitted values, severity column untouched; scope the npm claim to the one package swept and attribute any magnitude to its single lunation) so the builder's remaining work was mechanical application. attempts was 0, so the ladder gave no evidence to escalate on. The call did not hold: attempt 1 failed on execution of the pre-decided disposition, not on the decisions themselves. Recorded so the retro can weigh whether pre-deciding shrinks an item enough to keep it at haiku, or whether docs items on THIS repo should open at sonnet given two haiku doc failures in ten cycles (T-101 cycle 2, T-108 cycle 10).

decisions.what: the whole T-108 diff reverted rather than the two false sentences conductor-patched and the rest kept
decisions.why: Keeping the good two-thirds meant the conductor hand-writing the replacements for the exact two claims the gate had just judged - and cycle 7 established that a conductor editing the artifact leaves nothing independent checking the conductor's own wording. The salvage cost is real (a correct status-column table thrown away) and is paid down by describing every passing element in the retry brief, so attempt 2 reproduces them instead of rediscovering them. Same shape as cycle 7 -> 8 on T-103b, which landed on the retry.

decisions.what: the run's ONE review-fix pass is formally deferred pending an allocator posture change, and WRAP_UP reports it as NOT RUN rather than quietly omitting it
decisions.why: eleven consecutive cycles have deferred it for the same reason and the reason has not moved: review-fix is the most premium-heavy work type in the pipeline (reviewer opus, adversarial verifier fable) and allow_premium_pct has been 0 under trickle posture throughout. Gear 1's work-choice list (planning, backlog hygiene, docs, test triage, S-effort sonnet builds) does not include it, and the fable verifier seat CANNOT be demoted - the fable guard exempts judgment seats in every gear, which is correct: a cheap-tiered adversarial verifier is how a fake gate gets built. So there is no honest cheaper version to run. Recording it as a decision now, with ~19.7h to stop_at, so the morning report carries a deliberate deferral with a reason rather than an eleventh silent omission. If the posture leaves trickle before stop_at, this decision is superseded and the pass runs.

decisions.what: the 'module comment gloss wider than the code' pattern reached its FOURTH instance (T-110, T-112, T-113, now T-105) and is promoted from one-off backlog rows to a candidate playbook lesson for WRAP_UP distillation
decisions.why: T-113's own notes set the trigger: 'Third instance this run. If a fourth appears, the pattern is worth a playbook lesson rather than another one-off item.' T-105's gate hit it in a NEW form -- not a doc-comment glossing a constant, but a test comment claiming a cross-file coupling ('if that suite ever spawns a different file, this diverges and fails here first') that the code did not implement: it compared package.json against a second hardcoded copy of the same literal. Two conductor-authored mutants (repoint cli.test.js's BIN; repoint astro.test.js's require, manifest untouched) both SURVIVED the first draft, which is the empirical proof the coupling was decorative. The fix made the claim true rather than softening it -- the test now parses the sibling suites. The generalizable lesson is the mutant shape, not the wording: a comment asserting that A tracks B is testable by mutating B and leaving A alone, and a claim that survives that mutation is decoration.

decisions.what: T-110's fix accepted in the 'half-open range of years 1000-3000' framing rather than 'years 1000-2999', and the residual README readability question deliberately NOT filed as a fifth prose item
decisions.why: Two framings were true. 'Half-open' restates the bracket notation the repo already prints one line below in src/astro.js and introduces no new quantity; '2999' is a derived number that appears nowhere in the source, and this run's standing docs frame rule (cycles 2 and 4) says a quantity may appear only in the frame the repo already computes it in. The builder chose the framing that needs no new number and applied it identically at all three sites, which is the stronger reading of the rule. The residual I weighed and rejected: in README and REPORT the phrase stands without adjacent bracket notation, so a reader who does not know the term learns the extent but not which endpoint is open. That is a register question, not a truth question - the sentence is true as written, README's Accuracy section is already technical enough to discuss Meeus series and band discriminators, and the spec_digest names CHURN as this run's chief risk. Filing a fifth one-off prose row to re-word a true sentence is precisely the failure the digest warns against, so the gate passes and nothing is filed.

decisions.what: T-107's five success modes go in ONE table-driven test rather than five tests, and the exit-status assertion stays even though it is redundant
decisions.why: The builder chose the single-loop shape and argued the five modes share one behavioral claim; the conductor's mutation matrix confirms the loop genuinely reaches all five (M1-M5 each die only against the merged suite), so the compressed shape costs no coverage and the spec_digest names CHURN as this run's chief risk. The status assertion is kept with its redundancy DECLARED in the evidence file rather than quietly counted as new surface: M6 shows execFileSync already threw on non-zero exits pre-merge, so only the stderr half of the assertion is new coverage.

decisions.what: T-113 passed, and the fix was accepted in the framing that NAMES 0.88 at all three sites rather than a hedge like “nearly full”
decisions.why: The run’s standing docs frame rule (cycles 2 and 4) says a quantity may appear only in the frame the repo already computes it in, and 0.88 is not a derived figure — it is the literal in `else if (cover < 0.88) out += HALF`, one line below the comment being fixed. A hedge would have been the safer-looking choice and the worse one: it would have replaced an incomplete claim with a vague one, and this defect family is precisely prose drifting away from the branch it describes. The builder also wrote the raw fraction, not a percentage, which is the source’s own frame; “88%” would have been a re-expression the repo never computes.

decisions.what: the gate’s central check was an INSTRUMENTED SWEEP of the real branch, not a reading of the source — and it is what upgraded the item from ‘true by inspection’ to ‘true by measurement’
decisions.why: Reading `else if (cover < 0.88) HALF; else ROUND_LIMB` proves the fix is consistent with the source, but it does NOT prove the disc ever actually reaches that branch below full lit — if cover only ever hit 1.0 in practice, the old prose would have been complete after all and this item would have been churn. So renderLine was driven over a 20,000-step synodic sweep in both hemispheres against an instrumented COPY of render.js (repo source untouched): 2,924 of 33,192 round-limb draws land at cover<1.0, least-lit 0.887324. The sweep also checked the converse, which a one-directional check would have missed: outer cells with cover>=0.88 number EXACTLY 33,192, the same as the round-limb draws, so ‘0.88’ is the precise condition and not merely a sufficient one. Generalizable: a comment describing a branch is verifiable by instrumenting the branch and counting which side of it real inputs land on.

decisions.what: three gate flags (C4a, C4b, C4c) were traced to my own instrument and the instrument was repaired; each widening was paired with a strictly stronger assertion, and the normalizer was then falsified against HEAD
decisions.why: C4a swept `git ls-files`, so it flagged .swarm/backlog.json, .swarm/journal.md and the cycle-12 evidence file — the RECORD of the defect, which must keep the phrase ‘declines to establish’ to stay legible; product scope is src/, test/, README.md, REPORT.md, where the hit count is zero. C4b/C4c matched literal strings containing spaces while the edit had reflowed both passages, so ‘East Asian\nWidth class’ and ‘has not\n * been established’ spanned line breaks. Both are line-wrap blindness, the same class of instrument bug as cycle 8’s .trim() defect and cycle 9’s sentence-scope defect — third occurrence this run, and all three were MY regexes being narrower than the prose they measured. Guarding the repair the way cycles 8 and 9 did: C4a grew a volitional-verb family so a synonym cannot pass where the literal was caught; C4d now requires the test comment to assert README’s OWN predicate EXTRACTED from README rather than a string I chose, so the allowance cannot be something I invented; and C4f runs the normalized checks against HEAD and REQUIRES them to still catch the old wording — if prose() were manufacturing matches, C4f fails and the entire C4 block is void.

decisions.what: T-113 closes the fourth and last open instance of the ‘module doc-comment gloss wider than the code’ family (T-110, T-112, T-105, T-113); the candidate playbook lesson promoted at cycle 16 now has a complete case set for WRAP_UP distillation
decisions.why: Cycle 16 promoted the pattern to a candidate lesson on its fourth instance and named the generalizable test as the MUTANT shape (mutate B, leave A alone; a claim that survives is decoration). decisions.what: opened SPEC.md's Nice-to-haves gate and spent the cycle there (T-117, CI workflow) rather than on the one item the backlog actually held (T-116, British spellings)

decisions.what: verified T-117 by PUSHING it and reading GitHub's own execution log, not by reading the yaml
decisions.why: A workflow file is the one artifact where static review is systematically weakest: every wrong version of it is also well-formed yaml. The specific trap here was live -- this repo has no package-lock.json, so the near-universal `npm ci` idiom would have produced a workflow that parses, reviews clean, and fails on every run forever. Static checks caught that one because it was anticipated; the live run caught one that was NOT anticipated (the actions/*@v4 Node-20 runtime deprecation, T-118), which is the argument for the live run existing at all. The discriminator is the log line '# pass 114' from GitHub's runner: a vacuous, no-op, or invented-script workflow cannot emit this repo's exact test count from a machine the conductor does not control.

decisions.what: verified T-118 with a LIVE CONTROL rather than a single after-reading: queried the deprecation annotations on the v4 sha (12a6a70) and the v7 sha (c7b4cf2) through the same API call
decisions.why: 'zero annotations on the new run' is not evidence on its own - an empty annotations array is also what a broken query, a wrong check-run id, or a never-annotating repo returns. The v4 control returned the deprecation warning on BOTH legs through the identical call, so the empty result on v7 is a real difference in the artifact and not a silent failure of the measurement.

decisions.what: the gate's decisive check was a SOURCE mutation (nextFullMoon's target phase k+0.5 -> k+0.5001), not only mutations of the test's own constants.

decisions.what: My own first measurement said README's headline accuracy claim was FALSE. It was not -- the claim is true and my measurement was the wrong one. Caught by measuring a second and third way before filing anything.
decisions.why: README.md:164-165 and REPORT.md:34 both assert the implementation computes the 2000-01-06 new moon at 18:15 UTC. Bisecting the `age` discontinuity off the public surface gave 18:13:43.349Z -- which rounds to 18:14 and would have made the README's figure a fabrication of exactly the kind this run has removed eight times. Two further derivations refuted my own finding: bisecting the `cycleFraction` wrap (the method test/astro.test.js:63-72 itself uses) and, independently, ternary-searching the illumination MINIMUM (which comes from the ch.48 elongation series, not the ch.49 instant tables) both land on 18:15:22.79Z and agree with EACH OTHER to 4 milliseconds. The README is right. The root cause of my bad number is real and worth recording: `age` is computed at src/astro.js:313 from the ch.49 true-phase instant tables while `cycleFraction` is computed at src/astro.js:303 from the ch.48 elongation series, so the two zero 99.4 s apart -- the same two-series split KI-7 documents, showing up at an ordinary epoch rather than an absurd one. GENERALIZABLE, and it is the lesson of the cycle: a 'the docs are wrong' finding must be measured by the method the doc's own evidence uses AND by one method independent of it, because a single derivation off a different series is indistinguishable from a real defect. Evidence: .swarm/runs/cycle-029-anchor-measure.js.

Authored by the conductor BEFORE any builder started' -- so drift from it is expected and 'fixing' it would falsify the record of what was actually frozen. terminal font/width variance for the Unicode glyphs is an untested surface (taste judge, product-not-demo axis). No automated check can cover it; requires a human look.

Disc glyphs span two East Asian Width classes (U+2591 and U+2590 are Neutral; U+2592/3/2588/258C/258F/2595 are Ambiguous). In terminals that render ambiguous-width as double (CJK locales, iTerm2 ambiguous-as-double, xterm -cjk_width) the disc is 5-9 columns instead of 5: the single line jitters between nights, the two-line form stops aligning, and the --block frame does not close. Verified by measurement. Not a typo but an upstream Unicode fact - no Block Elements subset gives a 4-step ramp plus a symmetric half-block pair in one width class. Correct in default Western-locale terminals. Documented in README; fix needs a glyph-set redesign, deliberately deferred rather than rushed at the buzzer. MACHINE-PINNED at cycle 5 (T-104): test/render.test.js derives the disc's glyph alphabet from actual renderLine/renderBlock output and asserts it against the documented partition, so the defect can no longer drift silently - the fix (glyph-set redesign) remains deliberately deferred. The pin also EXPOSED a scope gap in the README's glyph list: the disc additionally draws U+25D6/U+25D7 (round limb), which the width caveat never mentions. Tracked as T-109. DOC SIDE CLOSED cycle 9 (T-109): the README's width caveat now scopes its Block Element claim precisely and accounts for the two round-limb glyphs it had omitted, without asserting an EAW class the repo cannot check. The underlying width defect is UNFIXED and still deferred - only the documentation gap closed. MACHINE-CHECKED AT CYCLE 24 (T-121), which settled the two things this entry had only ever ASSERTED. (1) The hand-typed Neutral/Ambiguous partition above is CORRECT: all 8 documented Block Element glyphs match unicodedata UCD 15.0.0 exactly, 0 disagreements in either direction, and the drawn alphabet parsed out of src/render.js equals the set test/render.test.js documents. (2) The impossibility claim ('no Block Elements subset gives a 4-step ramp plus a symmetric half-block pair in one width class') was ENUMERATED rather than reasoned, and HOLDS -- under both KI-5's literal wording and a wider predicate covering all three handed pairs the renderer actually draws, and under a search pool widened from Block Elements alone to Block Elements + Geometric Shapes + Symbols for Legacy Computing. The mechanism is now named exactly: U+258C LEFT HALF BLOCK is Ambiguous while U+2590 RIGHT HALF BLOCK is Neutral, and that is the ONLY LEFT/RIGHT HALF BLOCK pair in any of the three ranges -- so the split is not one option among several, it is the sole candidate. The Neutral class independently fails for a second reason: it contains no full-fill glyph at all (nearest miss U+1FB86 UPPER SEVEN EIGHTHS BLOCK, density 0.875), because Unicode never assigned these families a distinct fully-filled codepoint -- that would duplicate U+2588, which is Ambiguous. Verified non-vacuous: the SHIPPED glyph set does satisfy the predicate once the single-class constraint is dropped, so this is a real constraint result and not an impossible requirement. Nearest misses a human relaxing 'half-block' should look at first: U+25D0/U+25D1 (CIRCLE WITH LEFT/RIGHT HALF BLACK, both Ambiguous) and U+25E7/U+25E8 (SQUARE WITH LEFT/RIGHT HALF BLACK, both Neutral) are same-class L/R pairs, but are circle/square motifs rather than fractional blocks, and the Neutral ramp ceiling still blocks the square pair. LIMITS, stated rather than buried: UCD class is a Unicode property, NOT a promise about any particular terminal; the sweep covers three justified ranges on UCD 15.0.0, not all of Unicode; Unicode 16's Octant symbols postdate this data and were NOT checked. SEVERITY UNCHANGED at medium and the issue stays OPEN: nothing was fixed. What changed is that the deferral is now evidence-backed instead of assertion-backed.

At absurd epochs (+/-270,000 years) phaseName and illumination can contradict each other, because phaseName derives from the ch.49 instant tables and illumination from the ch.48 elongation series, and the two polynomials diverge. Zero contradictions across 350,592 states sampled over 2020-2040. Noted so it is not rediscovered as a live bug. BOUNDED (module half) at cycle 6 by T-103a: src/astro.js exports PHASE_ILLUMINATION_CONSISTENCY_DOMAIN declaring years 1000-3000, and test/astro.test.js samples 4000 deterministic points across it asserting the phase-name band discriminator (new below 0.10, crescents below 0.5, gibbous above 0.5, full above 0.90; quarters straddle and are exempt). Conductor-verified non-vacuous (3733 of 4000 samples reach a real assertion, all four bands exercised) and failable (widening the constant to year 80000 turns it red at +045200-07-01, proving the test reads the constant rather than a re-typed literal). Independently re-sampled at N=9973 and N=50021 on a jittered off-lattice: 0 violations. The bound is SAMPLED-clean, not proven, and is DECLARATIVE ONLY - nothing enforces it at runtime, deliberately, since a runtime guard is a behavior change the run's non-goals forbid. The README half LANDED at cycle 8 (T-103b attempt 2): README.md's ## Accuracy section now states the 1000-3000 domain, attributes it to test/astro.test.js as SAMPLED ('samples that domain and finds no contradiction'), and names the consequence of leaving it. The SPEC must-have 'KI-7 bounded by a declared+SAMPLED supported domain' is therefore SATISFIED. The issue stays OPEN at severity low because nothing was fixed: the two series still diverge at absurd epochs and the domain is declarative only. Bounded and documented is not the same as resolved. PROSE CORRECTED cycle 17 (T-110): all three sites that describe the domain (the src/astro.js doc comment, README's Accuracy paragraph, REPORT's KI-7 row) had glossed the half-open interval [Date.UTC(1000,0,1), Date.UTC(3000,0,1)) as an inclusive 'years 1000 through 3000' - one calendar year more than the constant defines and more than the test reaches (its last sample is 2999-07-02). All three now name the range as half-open, identically. The constant, the test, the stride and every assertion were left untouched; nothing about the issue itself changed.

package.json declares "license": "MIT" and "private": false, but the repo contains no LICENSE file (verified: no LICENSE* at the repo root). A repo that declares a license without shipping its text is legally ambiguous to the next person who wants to reuse it, and the audience for this run is explicitly 'the next person to change this code'. NOT fixed here on purpose: the MIT text needs a copyright holder line naming a legal person, which is the repo owner's decision and not one a build agent or the conductor may invent. Adjacent, separately tracked: T-116 notes README's '## Licence' heading disagrees with package.json's spelling. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the owner supplies the copyright line ('Copyright (c) <year> <holder>'); adding the standard MIT body around it is then a one-file mechanical change.
